question: How many moons does Mercury have, and what are their names?
answer:
Current scientific consensus is that Mercury has no confirmed natural satellites [1][2]. 

According to authoritative sources Mercury has zero moons, so there are no names to list [1][2]. 

In 1974 the Mariner 10 spacecraft detected an ultraviolet signal that was briefly interpreted as a possible moon, but the signal was later traced to the distant star 31 Crateris, disproving the claim [2]. 

Mercury’s lack of moons is explained by its small mass and extreme proximity to the Sun, which produce strong solar tidal forces, high solar radiation, a very small Hill sphere, and dynamical instabilities that make any captured or formed satellite unstable over long periods [1][2].

sources.title: Mercury Moons: Why the Swiftest Planet Stays Solitary (Science)
sources.snippet: Mercury Moons: Why the Swiftest Planet Stays Solitary (Science) April 02, 20267 minutes read Mercury has zero natural moons. Due to its extreme proximity to the Sun and its relatively small mass, the planet’s gravitational influence is too weak to maintain a stable orbit for any natural satellite. Understanding this lonely status requires exploring the complex gravitational environment of the inner solar system. … Why Mercury Has No Moons: The Gravitational Battle Key Takeaway: Mercury lacks moons because its Hill Sphere is too small, allowing the Sun’s massive gravity to hijack any potential satellites.  Mercury stands as a desolate exception in a solar system filled with diverse planetary satellites. … MESSENGER Mission Findings It took nearly four decades for NASA to return for a definitive census of the planet’s neighborhood. Between 2011 and 2015, the MESSENGER probe conducted an exhaustive survey while orbiting the planet, specifically hunting for Mercury’s missing moons. The mission employed high-resolution imaging and sensitive gravitational tracking to ensure that even a small, rogue asteroid captured by the planet would be detected. The analytical results were conclusive: the space surrounding the planet is remarkably empty. The mission confirmed that no natural satellites larger than 100 meters in diameter currently exist. This lack of companions is a direct consequence of the sun’s overwhelming gravitational influence, which effectively compresses the planet’s Hill Sphere and destabilizes any object that dares to linger. … Frequently Asked Questions: Mercury’s Solitary Journey Does Mercury have any natural moons? No, Mercury possesses zero natural moons. Despite its position as a major planet in our solar system, it remains a solitary world. This makes it one of only two planets in our celestial neighborhood without a natural satellite; the only other planet to share this moonless distinction is Venus. Why doesn’t Mercury have any moons? The primary reason for Mercury’s lack of companions is its extreme proximity to the Sun and its relatively small mass. The Sun’s massive gravitational pull dominates the region, leaving Mercury with a very compressed Hill Sphere—the volume of space where a planet’s gravity is strong enough to hold onto a moon. Because this zone is so small, any potential satellite would likely be stripped away by the Sun’s tidal forces or destabilized until it crashed into the planet’s surface.
